opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that there's no single correct balance, because it depends on what you want the model to be good at. The natural distribution of data on the internet is very different from the distribution of tasks people actually care about. If you just take everything in proportion to how much of it exists, you'll end up with a model that's heavily shaped by whatever happens to be abundant, and that may not be what your users need.

So I usually start from the target: what will this model be used for, and how will we measure success? From there, you can work backward and treat domain mixture as a real training parameter, almost like a hyperparameter, rather than an accident of data collection. You try different mixtures, evaluate on each domain separately, and look at the trade-offs. An aggregate score can hide a lot. Your overall number may go up while a smaller domain quietly gets worse.

The other important point is that more data from a domain doesn't translate linearly into better performance. There are often diminishing returns. Once a domain is reasonably covered, adding more may help very little, whereas a small amount of data from an underrepresented domain can make a big difference. Domains also interact. Some transfer well to each other, like data that teaches general reasoning skills helping across several areas, while others may mostly compete for the model's capacity and training time. Quality matters as well, so counting tokens or examples doesn't tell you the whole story.

In practice, it ends up being quite empirical. We have some intuitions, but I don't think we have a really principled theory yet for finding the optimal mixture. You run experiments, measure carefully per domain, and adjust. Honestly, I think this is an underappreciated research area, because people spend a lot of attention on architectures and algorithms, while the composition of the training data can have just as large an effect on what the model ends up being able to do.

r001.rationale: It says domains can compete for model capacity and training time, and that improving the aggregate score can coincide with worse performance in a smaller domain.

r002.rationale: It discusses choosing domain proportions, but does not propose setting domain granularity so the resulting domains have roughly comparable importance.

r003.rationale: It says quality matters and recommends empirical adjustment, but does not recommend equal mixing of high-quality data across equally important domains.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The honest answer is that data mixing is still more empirical than principled, but I think about it in a few layers.

The first thing is being clear about what you actually want the model to do. People sometimes treat the mixture as a neutral engineering knob, but it's really a statement of priorities. If you upweight code, you're saying you care about reasoning and structured outputs. If you upweight web text, you're saying you care about breadth and natural language. So before touching any ratios, I try to write down the target capabilities and the evaluations that reflect them.

The second layer is that domains interact in ways that aren't additive. A classic observation is that adding code helps on math and multi-step reasoning, even though those look like different domains on the surface. Conversely, adding a lot of one domain can quietly hurt another, and you only notice if you're tracking per-domain loss or downstream evals separately. So I always look at a matrix of domain-by-domain effects rather than a single aggregate number.

Third, I'm a big believer in doing this at small scale and then checking whether it transfers. You can run a lot of mixture sweeps with a model that's one or two orders of magnitude smaller than your final run. The rankings between mixtures tend to be fairly stable across scale, even if the absolute numbers aren't. That gives you a cheap way to prune bad choices. The caveat is that some effects, like long-tail knowledge or really hard reasoning, only show up at scale, so you still want a few checkpoints along the way where you revisit the decision.

There's also been nice work on treating this as an optimization problem, where you learn the weights by looking at which domains a proxy model struggles with, or by measuring how much each domain reduces loss on a held-out target. I like those approaches because they make the process less of a guessing game. But in practice I'd say they're a good starting point rather than the final word. They tend to find the mixture that minimizes average loss, and average loss is not always what you care about.

And the last piece, which I think gets underrated, is quality within a domain versus quantity across domains. A lot of the time the biggest gains don't come from shifting ratios between code and web, but from filtering and deduplicating within each bucket. Once the data is cleaner, the model becomes more forgiving about the exact proportions. So I spend as much effort on what's inside each domain as on how I balance them.

r001.rationale: The response says that adding a lot of one domain can hurt another, but does not state that finite training resources cause capability improvements to come at another capability’s expense.

r002.rationale: It discusses defining target capabilities and tracking domain effects, but does not recommend choosing domain granularity so the domains have roughly comparable importance.

r003.rationale: It recommends filtering and deduplicating data, but does not recommend equal mixing of high-quality data across domains judged equally important.

astra-6.text:
I think the first question is what you want the model to be good at. There isn’t necessarily one optimal mixture of data for every application. If you sample everything in proportion to how much data you have, the largest domain can dominate, but making every domain equally represented isn’t necessarily the right choice either.

I would treat the mixture as something you tune experimentally. Start with a reasonable balance, look at performance in each domain, and then adjust. You also want to understand whether adding data from one domain helps another domain or creates a trade-off. And data quality matters alongside quantity—a smaller amount of useful, diverse data can be more valuable than repeatedly sampling a large amount of redundant data.

r001.rationale: It mentions that adding data may create a trade-off, but does not state that finite training resources cause gains in one model capability to come at another capability’s expense.

r002.rationale: It discusses adjusting the mixture by domain performance, but does not propose choosing domain granularity to make domains roughly comparable in importance.

r003.rationale: It says quality matters and rejects equal representation as universally right, but does not recommend equally mixing high-quality data across domains of roughly equal importance.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first question is what you want the model to be good at. There isn’t necessarily one data mixture that’s best for every application. If you increase the proportion of one domain, you might improve performance there, but you also have to check what happens to the other domains.

So I would approach it empirically: start with a mixture, vary the proportions, and evaluate across the capabilities you care about. And I’d look at data quality as well as quantity. Having more examples from a domain doesn’t necessarily mean they’re contributing more useful information. The goal is to find a balance that supports the intended use of the model without letting one aggregate metric hide weaknesses elsewhere.

r001.rationale: It says increasing one domain’s share might improve that domain and prompts checking other domains, but does not state that finite training resources cause one capability’s improvement to come at another’s expense.

r002.rationale: It recommends varying domain proportions and evaluating capabilities, but does not propose choosing domain granularity to make domains roughly comparable in importance.

r003.rationale: It mentions data quality and finding a balance, but does not recommend equally mixing high-quality data across domains of roughly equal importance.
